parsed.explanation: The combined regime mixes a strongly protective division with a hostile national layer the division cannot displace. Locally, operative public-accommodation protections (retained by 67.8% ballot vote), gender-identity hate-crime coverage with a reporting unit, self-ID documents, and a healthcare shield law give outed travellers real recourse. Nationally, however, entry screening instructs officers to refuse on sex-discrepancy grounds with possible lifetime fraud findings, federal single-sex facilities are closed to trans users, and immigration custody has documented beatings, forced labour and sexual abuse of trans detainees. Courts have enjoined several orders, so remedies partially function. Street-level severity is low; border, federal-facility and custody exposures are tier 1–2 and contingent but documented. Net: above 0.55 anchors, below 0.75.

entry_documents.exposure: Feb 2025 cable tells officers to refuse cases where document discrepancy casts doubt on sex, and to weigh fraud findings carrying possible lifetime ineligibility; X markers halted; airport security outing via scanners/pat-downs documented. Applies at every crossing.
entry_documents.protection: Refusal is discretionary, requires all four fraud elements, has limited waivers, is never automatic, and is challenged in national courts; a legal-aid FAQ guides document strategy.
entry_documents.interaction: Division cannot alter federal entry screening; a locally protected visitor still faces the national border regime first.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: In immigration custody, trans men reported forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse, with guard statements mocking their gender; corrections bureau stopped reporting trans prisoner numbers from 2025.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Applies only if a visitor is detained; national courts have enjoined several orders and civil-society litigation is active, though custody oversight for trans detainees is not documented as working.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Entry refusal or overstay → immigration custody → documented abuse regime; the division's protections do not reach federal custody.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities; 22 units have building-wide or partial bans and 4 criminalise use in circumstances, but none of those bans is in this division. Federal buildings inside the division still fall under the national rule.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has no mapped facility ban; public-accommodation law (2016, ballot-confirmed) covers hotels, restaurants, shops and transport; a 2025 arrest case occurred elsewhere, not here.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Everyday venues are protected locally, but entering a federal building or national facility reactivates the exclusion.

care_services.exposure: National orders defund and stigmatise gender-affirming care, target under-18 care, and subpoena patient records; none of these bind this division's providers for adults.
care_services.protection: Division shield law (2022) protects patients and providers from out-of-jurisdiction charges — directly useful to visitors from banning units — plus codified 2022 care protections and a conversion-therapy ban; listing current to Sept 2026.
care_services.interaction: A visitor's home-unit ban cannot be used against care received here, but federal funding and record-subpoena powers remain national exposures.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National rhetoric: 'gender ideology' removed from agencies, orders framing care as 'mutilation', counterterrorism strategy naming 'radically pro-transgender' groups, and a reward memo citing 'radical gender ideology'; 66% nationally back birth-sex markers on documents.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Division hate-crime statute covers gender identity (2012) with a police/justice/legislative reporting unit and task force; state officials here enacted protective laws repeatedly since 2011.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hostile federal framing raises street-level odds of confrontation while local law enforcement and prosecutors remain protective.

minors_guardians.exposure: National orders direct law-enforcement investigation and criminal prosecution of teachers facilitating a trans minor's social transition, and youth care is banned in 27 units; a travelling parent with a trans minor may face federal facility rules and scrutiny.
minors_guardians.protection: In this division a minor accompanying a protected adult uses the same public-accommodation and shield protections; no division-level youth-care or social-transition ban is documented.
minors_guardians.interaction: Protection is local; if the family crosses into a banning unit or a federal setting, the hostile rules apply.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No division-specific anti-trans violence incidents are documented; national bias statistics and 190+ anti-trans bills show climate friction, and 37 units lack GI bias statutes — none of which binds here.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Operative GI hate-crime law with mandatory incident collection and public reporting, plus employment/housing/public-accommodation protections; national hate-crimes statute also covers gender identity.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Local police and reporting machinery are functional, so an assaulted visitor has a credible path to recourse.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Sodomy-era provisions remain unrepealed (unenforceable since 1974, so tangential); national orders are partly blocked, partly in force, making border outcomes time-dependent; several legislative dates rest on secondary sources.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Working courts have enjoined multiple orders; division remedies include a hate-crime reporting unit, enforcement of public accommodations, a 'Most Protective' tier ranking (July 2026) and confidential name changes.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Rule of law here cuts for trans travellers locally, but cannot stay federal entry or custody practice.

anchor_checks.comparison: Vellandra bars all trans visitors routinely with no real appeal. Here the national cable enables refusal on sex-doubt grounds and threatens fraud findings, but refusal is discretionary, elements are strict, waivers exist, and courts are actively reviewing — a real but far less absolute exposure than a blanket register.

Kestrel Isles' discretionary secondary screening with slow, rarely revised appeals closely matches this dossier's border axis. This case rates higher because the division adds operative public-accommodation, hate-crime and shield protections with functioning remedies, which Kestrel's visitor lacks at street level.

Vellmaris shows brief document-mismatch detention, intervention by an advocacy group, apology and compensation — mirroring the friction-plus-working-remedy pattern here. This rates slightly below because the national layer adds documented trans abuse in immigration custody and federal facility exclusion, absent in Vellmaris.

Meridia's trained, respectful border inspection and low detention severity exceed this dossier: the national cable instructs suspicion and refusal rather than respectful handling, and custody abuse of trans detainees is documented. Local protections, however, match this tier, so the case sits a step below.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller meets two regimes in sequence. At the border and in federal facilities or custody, the hostile national layer governs: sex-doubt refusals with possible lifetime fraud findings, exclusion from federally funded single-sex facilities, and documented beatings, forced labour and sexual abuse of trans immigration detainees — though several orders are enjoined and fraud findings are never automatic. Once inside the division, protections are unusually strong and operative: ballot-confirmed public accommodations, gender-identity hate-crime coverage with a functioning reporting unit, self-ID documents, and a shield law covering visitors' care. Local rule of law therefore mitigates street, service and care exposure substantially, while border, federal-building and detention exposures remain unmitigated, producing a protective-but-conditional mid-range rating.
